claims.text: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 aged at approximately 600°C exhibits a brittle window.
The brittle window occurs when L12 ordering in the FCC matrix approaches a critical, near-stoichiometric Ni3Al state.
Near-stoichiometric L12 ordering maximizes the antiphase boundary energy.
High antiphase boundary energy suppresses dislocation cross-slip and forces planar slip.
Aging at approximately 600°C produces a high density of Ni3Al-type L12 ordered domains in the FCC matrix.
Aging at approximately 600°C produces jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries.
Jagged B2/FCC boundaries act as geometric stress concentrators.
Planar slip bands interacting with jagged B2/FCC interfaces cause crack initiation and loss of ductility.
Aging at approximately 750°C decreases the L12 order parameter and consequently lowers the antiphase boundary energy.
Aging at approximately 750°C smooths the B2/FCC interfaces, permits cross-slip and strain hardening, and restores ductility.
The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has a ductile FCC matrix containing B2 precipitates, with high elongation and low yield strength.
Tensile elongation has a distinct minimum near 600°C that coincides with maximum antiphase boundary energy and maximum jagged-interface density.
The 600°C-aged state has higher nanoindentation hardness than the 750°C-aged state.
The 600°C-aged state has a lower nanoindentation pop-in load than the 750°C-aged state, and this lower load indicates restricted dislocation nucleation.
The brittle transition requires both an L12 ordering parameter above a critical value and B2/FCC interface roughness above a critical value.
Antiphase boundary energy can be inferred from dislocation dissociation width measured by TEM.
The critical L12 ordering parameter and quantitative wavelength or amplitude defining a jagged interface are not specified.

contradictions.description: The mechanism presents high APBE as a barrier that restricts dislocation activity, but the predicted lower pop-in load at 600°C is interpreted as restricted dislocation nucleation. A lower pop-in load ordinarily means that the first plastic event occurs at a lower applied load, so the stated direction does not coherently represent an increased nucleation barrier.
